title: Charlie Shavers in the Dorsey band and race in the band
summary: Asked about Charlie Shavers as the one black player in the Dorsey band, he recalls the Marie arrangement and says race meant little to him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you a question, sort of rewind. You saw Charlie Shavers in the Dorsey band just down the street from here. Was there any — of course you were pretty young — but was there any significance to the fact that here’s this black man playing, who probably was the only black person in the band, right?
That’s correct. Except for Pearl Bailey, who was not in the band.
In the car. Do you remember that? Any significance to that?

I remember that what they had done was — the hit song that he had at that time — no I mean Tommy Dorsey had a couple of hits. One was “Song of India” and the other was “Marie.” But what they had done was they had transcribed Bunny Berigan’s original chorus on “Marie” for the entire trumpet section. And man, when Charlie Shavers hit that night with that, I’m not sure that he had the lead part or not — I wouldn’t be surprised but what he didn’t — but when he did it just blew the place apart. Man, you know, like whether he took it up an octave I can’t remember because that’s so far in the past. But I knew that he — and then he — I’m not sure if he came down to play with the Clambake Seven or Lee Castle might have. No Charlie Shavers came down when they broke down — it was a band within the band. You know they used to have bands within the bands.
I didn’t think much about it, black or white, especially when I got in the Army.
